LESSONS.title: Variables are labels
LESSONS.goal: Give a value a name and use it again
summary: A variable is a name label stuck on a value
= sticks the name on the left to the value on the right
Assign again and the label moves to the new value

cards.say: A variable is a name label you stick on a value. = doesn't mean “equals” here. It means “stick the name on the left onto the value on the right.” Once it's stuck, just call the name and you get the value.

Assign to the same name again and the label moves to the new value; the old one is forgotten. The right side is worked out first, so a line like money = money - 4500 makes sense. Your math teacher would not approve.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A label sits on only one value at a time. On line 2 it moved to 1600, so bus is now 1600.

items.q: Fill in the blank to put “gimbap” (Korean rice rolls) into the variable menu.
items.explain: To store a value you use a single =. == asks “are these two values the same?” and you'll meet it again in Chapter 3.

items.q: Which line runs without an error?
items.explain: The name goes on the left of =, the value on the right. You can't stick a label on a number or a string, so the other two give a SyntaxError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: b = a sticks a second label, b, on the value a had at that moment: 3. Moving a to 10 later doesn't move b. It stays on 3.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The right side x + 1 is worked out first to make 6, then the x label moves onto that 6. This line works because = isn't the math “equals.”

items.q: You have 10000 won of pocket money and spend 3000. Put the lines in order to print what's left.
items.explain: You can only call a label after it's stuck on. Stick it → move it to the new value → print, so you get 7000.

items.task: You bought 3 cup noodles at 1300 won each at a convenience store. Put the price in a variable named price and the number in a variable named count, then print price times count. Don't type 3900 yourself!
hints: Read the task again: the price is 1300 won and you bought 3. You need two variables, price and count.
= sticks the name on the left onto the value on the right. Calling the name gives you the value. Think back to the first card.
Make one more variable, count, under price, then multiply the two names with * inside print's parentheses.

price = 1300
count = ___
print(price ___ count)
items.explain: With names on the values, the line reads as “price × count.” If the count changes, you only fix the count line.

items.q: Which statement about variables is true?
options: = sticks the left name on the right value
= is the math sign for “both sides are equal”
Once a value is stored, it can't change
items.explain: = sticks on a label. Assign to the same name again and the label moves to the new value.

LESSONS.title: Kinds of values: types
LESSONS.goal: Tell int, float and str apart and check with type()
summary: Whole numbers are int, decimals are float, text is str
type() tells you what kind a value is
Dividing with / always gives a float
round(value, digits) rounds to that many decimals

cards.say: Values come in kinds. A whole number like 3 is an int, a decimal like 3.5 is a float, and anything in quotes is a string, str. Put a value in type() and it tells you the kind.
Divide with / and 7 / 2 is 3.5. Even 8 / 2, which divides evenly, is 4.0. The result of / is always a float. If you need a whole number, use // from Chapter 1.
Sometimes decimals go on and on, like 10 / 3. round(value) rounds to the nearest whole number, and round(value, 2) keeps two decimal places.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: It's a whole number with no decimal point and no quotes, so it's an int. Exact amounts like a bus fare are usually ints.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The kind belongs to the value, not the label. The value on temp, 21.5, has a decimal point, so it's a float.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints <class 'str'>.
items.explain: Wrap it in quotes and it's a str, even if it looks like a number. 7 is an int and 7.0 is a float.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The result of / is a float even when it divides evenly, so you get 2.0 with a decimal point.

items.q: Which of these makes a value of type float?
items.explain: 10 / 5 is 2.0, a float. 10 // 5 is the whole-number quotient of two ints, so it's the int 2, and "2.0" has quotes, so it's a str.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the output is int, float, str.
items.explain: 5 is an int, 5 / 1 used / so it's a float, and "5" has quotes so it's a str. Same 5, different kinds depending on how you write it.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 2 / 3 is a long 0.666…. round(value, 2) keeps two decimal places, and since the third digit is 6 it rounds up to 0.67.

items.task: Let's build a weather app! Put today's temperature, 18.5, in a variable temp. On line 1 print the value of temp, and on line 2 print temp's type using type(). The output is two lines: 18.5 and <class 'float'>.
hints: The output is two lines. Line 1 is 18.5 and line 2 is <class 'float'>.
type() tells you a value's kind. Give it a variable and it tells you the kind of the value that label is on.
Print the value with print(temp), then below it put type(temp) inside another print.

temp = 18.5
print(___)
print(type(___))
items.explain: type(temp) told you the kind of 18.5, the value on temp. It has a decimal point, so it's a float.

items.q: Which statement about types is true?
options: "10" is an int even with quotes
items.explain: The result of / is always a float, so 8 / 2 is 4.0. "10" in quotes is a str.

LESSONS.title: Ask and listen: input
LESSONS.goal: Take what the user types with input() and use it
summary: input() waits for typing, then hands it back
What you get back is always a str (string)
A question in the parentheses shows up first

cards.say: When Python meets input(), it stops and waits. Press Enter and it hands back what you typed as a string (str). On this card we typed “latte”. Put a question inside, like input("Menu? "), and it shows before you type.
Important! input() always hands back a str, even if you type a number. So if you get 2 and do * 2, you get 22, not 4. You'll learn to turn it into a number in the next lesson.

items.q: If you type Ria, what's the output?
items.explain: The name label goes on “Ria,” the value input() handed back. name without quotes is a label, so it's swapped for its value.

items.q: If you type 5, what's the output?
items.explain: input() hands back a str no matter what you type. Type 5 and you get the string (str) "5".

items.q: If you type 3, what's the output?
items.explain: The value is the string (str) "3". A string * 2 repeats it, so you get 33, not 6.

items.q: In input("Menu? "), what does the string in the parentheses do?
options: It's a question shown before typing
It's the value used if nothing is typed
It's the variable name for the input
items.explain: The string in the parentheses is a question shown on screen before Python waits for input. Labeling the value is the job of the variable left of =.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “, hi!” comes right after the name you type.
items.explain: What input() hands back is a str too, so you can join it to another string with +. Strings can't be subtracted, and * needs a number.

items.q: Put the lines in order so typing Ria prints two lines: “Hi, Ria!” and “Come on in.”
items.explain: Take the input first and stick the name label on it; only then can you call that name. After that, place the prints in the order they should appear.

items.task: Let's make a cafe “order ready” call! Take a customer's name with input() and print “NAME, your drink is ready”. Typing Ria gives “Ria, your drink is ready”. Leave input()'s parentheses empty for grading.

tests.expect: Saessak Kim, your drink is ready

hints: One name goes in, one line comes out. Right after the name comes “, your drink is ready” with the comma touching the name.
input() hands back what you typed as a string (str). Strings can be joined with +.
Inside print, join the value on name and “, your drink is ready” with +. If you type Ria directly, it breaks for the next customer.

name = input()
print(name + "___")
items.solution:
name = input()
print(name + ", your drink is ready")
items.explain: You stuck the name label on what input() handed back and joined the message with +. Now it calls out whoever shows up.

items.q: Which statement about input() is true?
options: It hands back a str even for numbers
It hands back an int if you type a number
It moves on without waiting for input
items.explain: input() waits until you press Enter, then always hands back what you typed as a string (str). To do math, you have to turn it into a number.

LESSONS.title: Type conversion
LESSONS.goal: Change a value's kind with int(), float() and str()
summary: int("3") is 3, float("2.5") is 2.5
str(500) is the string "500"
str + int is a TypeError, so convert first

cards.say: The value from input() is a string (str), so you can't do math with it. int() turns it into a whole number, float() into a decimal (type conversion). In int(input()), the inner input() runs first, then int() turns its result into a number.

Join a string (str) and a number with + and you get a TypeError. Wrap the number in str() to make it a string, and they join. You can also pass them to print separated by a comma, but then you get one space in between.
cards.code:
total = 9000
print("Total " + str(total) + " won")
print("Total", total)

items.q: Which code causes an error?
items.explain: str + int mixes two kinds, so it's a TypeError. Turning 20 into a string with str(), or separating with a comma, works fine.

items.q: If you type 1 and then 2, what's the output?
items.code:
a = input()
b = input()
print(int(a) + int(b))
items.explain: int() turned both into numbers, so it's real addition: 3. Without converting, the strings would be joined into 12.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints “Total 9000 won”.
items.explain: To join it with strings, the number has to become a string, so it's str(). int() or float() keep it a number, which gives a TypeError.

items.q: Which code causes an error?
items.explain: int() can't turn the string "3.5", which has a decimal point, into a whole number, so it's a ValueError. float("3.5") is 3.5, and int(3.5) drops the decimals to give 3.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: int() doesn't round; it just drops everything after the decimal point. So even 7.9 becomes 7.

items.q: Put the lines in order so typing 3 prints the bus fare, 4500.
items.explain: The "3" you get must become an int before you multiply. Multiply first and the string "3" gets repeated 1500 times.

items.task: Bus fare calculator! The fare is 1500 won per person. Take the number of people with input() and print “Fare N won”. Typing 3 gives “Fare 4500 won”. Leave input()'s parentheses empty for grading.
hints: The output looks like “Fare 4500 won”: exactly one space on each side of the number.
The value from input() is a str, so you need int() to multiply. To join the result with strings, wrap it in str() again.
Turn the number of people into an int and multiply by 1500, then wrap that in str() and join it between “Fare ” and “ won” with +.

people = int(input())
fare = people * ___
print("Fare " + ___(fare) + " won")
items.solution:
people = int(input())
fare = people * 1500
print("Fare " + str(fare) + " won")
items.explain: You converted with int() to calculate, then back with str() to join the sentence. Numbers for math, strings for showing.

items.q: Which statement about type conversion is true?
items.explain: A string with a decimal point can't go straight through int(). "3" + 4 is a TypeError, and str(500) is the string "500".

LESSONS.title: Chapter 2 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Use variables, types, input and conversion together
summary: A variable is a label; = sticks it on
input() always hands back a str
int() for math, str() for joining strings

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 2. Labels, kinds of values, input and conversion are all on one screen. Follow whether each line's value is a str or an int, and you're ready.
cards.code:
cups = input()
price = 4500
total = int(cups) * price
print("Total " + str(total) + " won")

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
cup = 2
cup = cup + 1
cup = cup * 2
print(cup)
items.explain: Start at 2, add 1 to get 3, then multiply that 3 by 2 to get 6. On each line the label moves to the new value.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 10 / 2 is 5.0. The result of / is a float even when it divides evenly.

items.q: If you type 4, what's the output?
items.explain: The "4" from input() is a string (str), so + joins. If you wanted 8, convert with int() first.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: It has quotes, so price is a str. A string * 2 repeats it, giving 45004500.

items.q: Fill in the blank so typing 2 prints 9000.
items.explain: To multiply, the string "2" has to become the whole number 2 with int(). str() keeps it a string, so 2 would be repeated 4500 times.

items.q: Which code causes an error?
items.explain: str + float is a TypeError. Wrapping it in str() to make a string, or using float() to do math with numbers, works fine.

items.q: Put the lines in order so typing 4000 prints “Money left 6000”.
items.explain: Take the input as a number → work out what's left → turn it into a string and print. A label can only be called after it's stuck on.

items.task: Let's build a coffee bill calculator! Take the number of americanos (4000 won) and then lattes (4500 won) with input(), and print “Total N won”. Typing 2 and 1 gives “Total 12500 won”. Leave input()'s parentheses empty.
hints: There are two inputs: first the americano count, then the latte count. Swap them and the total changes.
input() hands back a str, so you need int() to multiply. To join with strings, change it back with str().
Convert both counts with int(), add up count × price into total, then join it between “Total ” and “ won”.

americano = int(input())
latte = int(input())
total = americano * 4000
total = total + latte * ___
print("Total " + ___(total) + " won")
items.solution:
americano = int(input())
latte = int(input())
total = americano * 4000
total = total + latte * 4500
print("Total " + str(total) + " won")
items.explain: You turned the counts into numbers with int(), built up the sum by moving the total label, and joined it into a sentence with str(). A real calculator that works for any input.

items.q: Which statement about Chapter 2 is true?
options: input() values need int() for math
x = x + 1 is wrong, so it errors
items.explain: input() always gives a str, so convert with int() before math. x = x + 1 moves a label, 7 / 2 is 3.5, and "5" + 5 is a TypeError.

ADVANCED.title: Tiny decimal errors
ADVANCED.goal: Know the 0.1 + 0.2 error and tidy it with round
summary: Decimals are stored as very close values
So a tiny error can tag along at the end
round(value, digits) tidies it up

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Remember round from 2-2? You'd think 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3, but a computer can't hold 0.1 exactly, so it holds a value very close to it. It's not a bug!
The error is tiny, but it looks odd on screen. round(value, digits) decides how many decimal places to keep and rounds to the nearest value. The rounded result is still a float.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 0.1 and 0.2 don't come out even in binary, so they're stored as very close values. Add them and a tiny error tags along at the end.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: round(value, 2) keeps two decimal places. The third digit, 1, isn't enough to round up, so it's 3.14.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints 3.1.
items.explain: To keep one decimal place, use 1. 2 gives 3.14 and 3 gives 3.142.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: round only rounds the number; it doesn't add zeros to fill a format. 7.0 is a float, so it prints as 7.0.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 1.1 + 2.2 is 3.3000000000000003, but rounding to one decimal place tidies it into a clean 3.3.

items.q: Put the lines in order so 0.7 + 0.1 is tidied and prints 0.8.
items.explain: Label the sum → tidy it with round and move the label → print. Print before tidying and you get 0.7999999999999999.

items.task: Shopping basket weight! Take two item weights (kg) one after another with float(input()), add them, round to two decimal places and print. Typing 0.1 and 0.2 gives 0.3. Leave input()'s parentheses empty.
hints: Two weights go in, one sum comes out. Because of the tiny error, just adding 0.1 and 0.2 doesn't give 0.3.
The tool that decides how many decimal places to keep was round(value, digits). For two places, digits is 2.
Put the sum of the two variables first in round, the number of places second, and print it.

a = float(input())
b = float(input())
print(round(a ___ b, ___))
items.solution:
a = float(input())
b = float(input())
print(round(a + b, 2))
items.explain: You read floats, added them and tidied with round(…, 2). Now the error tail disappears no matter what's typed.

items.q: Which statement about decimal math is true?
options: Tiny errors can appear, so tidy with round
round(value, 2) turns it into an int
items.explain: Decimals are stored as close binary values, so a tiny error can tag along. Rounding a float with round(value, 2) still gives a float.

ADVANCED.title: Using // and %
ADVANCED.goal: Split things like time with //, % and divmod
summary: // gives the quotient, % the remainder
divmod(a, b) gives both at once
Unpack them with h, m = divmod(t, 60)

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. How many hours and minutes is 130 minutes? Get the hours with // and the leftover minutes with %. The remainder % shows up all the time in clock math.

You often need the quotient and remainder together, so divmod(a, b) gets both at once. Write h, m = divmod(130, 60) and the quotient gets the h label, the remainder gets m. Just remember: two names with a comma.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Take 5 out of 17 three times and 2 is left. % gives you that leftover: the remainder.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 75 divided by 60 is 1 with 15 left over. The quotient goes on h and the remainder on m, so printing m gives 15.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints 3.
items.explain: 200 divided by 60 is 3 with 20 left over. The quotient goes on the first name, h, so print(h) gives 3.

items.q: When the integer n is even, what is n % 2?
items.explain: An even number divides by 2 evenly, so the remainder is 0. For an odd number it's 1.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A clock wraps around after 12. 15 divided by 12 leaves 3, so 5 hours after 10 o'clock is 3 o'clock.

items.q: Put the lines in order so typing 135 prints the leftover minutes, 15.
items.explain: Take the input as a number → split it with divmod → print the remainder m. 135 minutes is 2 hours 15 minutes.

items.task: Study time converter! Take the minutes studied with input() and print them as hours and minutes, like “2h 10m”. Use divmod; typing 130 gives “2h 10m”. Leave input()'s parentheses empty.
hints: One number of minutes goes in. Every 60 minutes is an hour, so the quotient is the hours and the remainder is the leftover minutes.
divmod(a, b) gives the quotient and remainder at once. Catch them as h, m = divmod(…).
Split total by 60 with divmod into two names. Turn each into a str, join them with “h ” and “m”, then print.

total = int(input())
h, m = divmod(total, ___)
print(str(h) + "h", str(m) + "___")
items.solution:
total = int(input())
h, m = divmod(total, 60)
print(str(h) + "h", str(m) + "m")
items.explain: divmod(total, 60) gave the hours and leftover minutes in one go. It's right even under an hour, like 45, or on the dot, like 60.

items.q: Which statement about divmod is true?
options: divmod(a, b) gives quotient and remainder
divmod(a, b) gives only the remainder
divmod(a, b) multiplies a and b
items.explain: divmod(a, b) gives a // b and a % b together. Unpack the two values with h, m = divmod(…).

ADVANCED.title: Unit converter
ADVANCED.goal: Build a unit converter with round and divmod
summary: miles × 1.609 is km; tidy it with round
Split seconds with divmod(sec, 60)
Both Deep Dive tools in one program

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. Time to put things to use! 1 mile is about 1.609 km, so just multiply. Multiplying decimals can leave messy digits at the end, and that's round's cue.
Splitting seconds into minutes and seconds is divmod's turn. 200 seconds divided by 60 is 3 minutes with 20 seconds left. round for decimals, divmod for splitting, and your converter is done.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 2 × 1.609 is 3.218, and rounding to two decimal places gives 3.22, because the third digit, 8, rounds up.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints 2 5.
items.explain: 125 seconds is 2 minutes 5 seconds. The quotient is m and the remainder is s, so print(m, s) prints “2 5” with a space from the comma.

items.q: Put the lines in order so typing 200 prints two lines: 3 and 20.
items.explain: Take the seconds → split into minutes and seconds with divmod → print minutes, then seconds. Swap them and 20 comes first.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 1.609 × 5 is about 8.045. Rounded to one decimal place it's 8.0, and rounding a float gives a float, so the decimal point stays.

items.q: Why use round when turning miles into km?
options: To tidy long decimal digits after multiplying
To make it an int and drop the decimal point
items.explain: Multiplying decimals can leave long tails or tiny errors, so round tidies them for display. It doesn't turn the value into an int.

items.task: Travel unit converter! Take miles with float(input()), then seconds with int(input()). Line 1: miles × 1.609 rounded to two places as “N km”. Line 2: use divmod to print minutes and seconds, like “3m 20s”. 3 and 200 give “4.83 km” and “3m 20s”. Leave input()'s parentheses empty.
hints: Two inputs, miles and seconds, and two lines out. Line 1 is km, line 2 is minutes and seconds.
You tidy decimals with round(value, digits) and split into quotient and remainder with divmod. Both are tools from this lesson.
Multiply miles by 1.609, tidy with round and join “ km”. For seconds, divmod by 60 and join the minutes and seconds.

km = round(miles * ___, 2)
print(str(km) + " km")
m, s = divmod(sec, ___)
print(str(m) + "m", str(s) + "s")
items.solution:
miles = float(input())
sec = int(input())
km = round(miles * 1.609, 2)
print(str(km) + " km")
m, s = divmod(sec, 60)
print(str(m) + "m", str(s) + "s")
items.explain: round tidied the decimal tail of km, and divmod split the seconds into minutes and seconds. Both Deep Dive tools worked together in one program.

items.q: Which statement about this lesson's converter is true?
options: round for decimals, divmod for splitting
divmod for decimals, round for splitting
It used only round for both
items.explain: round tidied the decimal tail of miles × 1.609, and divmod did the job of splitting seconds into minutes and seconds.

TEMPLATES.q: A coin piggy bank. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: The right side (coins + {B}) is worked out first, then that value goes back into coins. "coins" in quotes isn't the variable; it's just text.

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so the age, stored as text, becomes an integer and gets 1 added.
TEMPLATES.explain: A number in quotes is text. You need int() to make it an integer before adding 1. float() would give a value with a decimal point.
A number in quotes is text. Text * 2 joins it twice; a number * 2 multiplies. So the screen shows {OUT}.

TEMPLATES.q: You typed two numbers, one after another. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.code:
a = input()
b = input()
print(a + b)
wrong:
a = input()
b = input()
print(int(a) + int(b))

a = input()
b = input()
print(a, b)
TEMPLATES.explain: A value from input() is always text. + between texts joins them, so it doesn't add.
